notes:
Nomenclature & classes

  • Alcohols R–OH: 1°, 2°, 3° by the carbon bearing OH. Phenols: OH directly on aromatic ring (sp$^2$ C–OH). Ethers: R–O–R' (simple or mixed).

Preparation

  • Alcohols: hydration of alkenes (Markovnikov, acid-catalysed), from Grignard + carbonyl compound, reduction of aldehyde/ketone/acid (LiAlH$_4$/NaBH$_4$), hydroboration-oxidation (anti-Markovnikov).
  • Phenols: from haloarenes (fused NaOH, high T/P), from diazonium salts (hydrolysis), from cumene (cumene process — industrial; also gives acetone as by-product).
  • Ethers: Williamson synthesis, R–O$^-$Na$^+$ + R'–X → R–O–R' (S$_N$2; best with 1° R'X); dehydration of alcohols (140°C, conc. H$_2$SO$_4$).

Physical properties

PropertyTrend/reason
B.p. of alcoholshigher than alkanes/ethers of similar mass — H-bonding; decreases with branching
Acidity: alcohol vs phenol vs waterphenol > water > alcohol (phenoxide stabilised by resonance)
Acidity of substituted phenols–NO$_2$ (o/p) increases acidity; –CH$_3$/–OCH$_3$ (o/p, +I/+R) decreases it

Reactions of alcohols

  • With Na: 2ROH + 2Na → 2RONa + H$_2$↑ (test for –OH).
  • Esterification with acids/anhydrides (conc. H$_2$SO$_4$); Oxidation: 1° → aldehyde → acid (with KMnO$_4$/acidic K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$); 2° → ketone; 3° resists oxidation (no α-H) but is cleaved under strong conditions.
  • Lucas test: 3° alcohol turns turbid immediately, 2° in a few minutes, 1° only on heating — distinguishes classes.
  • Dehydration: conc. H$_2$SO$_4$, 443 K → alkene (Saytzeff, follows 3° > 2° > 1° ease, via carbocation for 2°/3°).

Reactions of phenols

  • Acidic: reacts with NaOH to form sodium phenoxide (but not with NaHCO$_3$ — weaker acid than carbonic acid).
  • Electrophilic substitution (o,p-directing, activating): bromination with Br$_2$ water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white ppt, test for phenol); nitration; Kolbe's reaction (CO$_2$/NaOH → salicylic acid); Reimer–Tiemann reaction (CHCl$_3$/NaOH → salicylaldehyde).
  • Azo coupling with diazonium salts gives coloured azo dyes.

Reactions of ethers

  • Cleavage by excess HI/HX: gives alkyl halide + alcohol/phenol (aryl ethers give phenol, not aryl halide, since aryl–O bond resists cleavage). With excess HI both C–O bonds cleave.
  • Ethers are fairly unreactive (used as solvents); form peroxides on standing in air (explosion hazard — test with FeSO$_4$/KSCN).

Exam tip

3–4 questions typical: acidity order (phenol > alcohol; effect of substituents), Lucas test, distinguishing 1°/2°/3° alcohols, Williamson synthesis and ether cleavage, and one named reaction (Kolbe/Reimer–Tiemann).

questions.q: The correct order of acidity is
questions.explanation: The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance with the ring, making phenol more acidic than water, which in turn is more acidic than ethanol (no such stabilisation, +I effect of ethyl raises electron density on O).
questions.trick: Acidity: phenol $>$ water $>$ ethanol (phenoxide resonance-stabilised).

questions.q: p-Nitrophenol is more acidic than phenol because the nitro group
options: withdraws electrons by resonance and induction, stabilising the phenoxide ion
donates electrons by resonance, stabilising phenoxide
questions.explanation: –NO$_2$ at the para position withdraws electron density through resonance and induction, delocalising the negative charge of the phenoxide ion and stabilising it, so p-nitrophenol is a stronger acid.
questions.trick: EWG (-NO$_2$) at o/p stabilises phenoxide by resonance $\to$ more acidic.

questions.q: The Lucas test distinguishes 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols based on
options: rate of turbidity formation with conc. HCl/ZnCl$_2$ (S$_N$1 reactivity)
questions.explanation: 3° alcohols form the more stable carbocation fastest and turn turbid immediately; 2° take a few minutes; 1° alcohols react only on heating.
questions.trick: Lucas: turbidity speed tracks carbocation stability, 3$^\circ$ instant, 1$^\circ$ on heating.

questions.q: Williamson's synthesis of an unsymmetrical ether R–O–R' proceeds via
options: S$_N$2 attack of alkoxide ion on a primary alkyl halide
questions.explanation: Sodium alkoxide (nucleophile) attacks a primary (or methyl) alkyl halide in an S$_N$2 mechanism; a bulky/3° halide would instead undergo elimination.
questions.trick: Williamson: alkoxide + 1$^\circ$ RX via S$_N$2; 3$^\circ$ RX gives elimination instead.

questions.q: Anisole (methoxybenzene) on treatment with excess HI gives
questions.explanation: The alkyl–oxygen bond cleaves (aryl–oxygen bond resists S$_N$2/S$_N$1 due to partial double bond character), giving phenol and methyl iodide.
questions.trick: Aryl ethers cleave at alkyl-O bond with HI, keeping Ar-O intact $\to$ phenol + RI.

questions.q: Which of the following would liberate CO$_2$ gas from sodium bicarbonate solution?
questions.explanation: Benzoic acid (a carboxylic acid, pKa ≈ 4) is a stronger acid than carbonic acid and liberates CO$_2$ from NaHCO$_3$; phenol (pKa ≈ 10) is too weak to do so.
questions.trick: Only acids stronger than carbonic acid fizz with NaHCO$_3$; phenol is too weak.

questions.q: Kolbe's reaction converts sodium phenoxide into
questions.explanation: Sodium phenoxide + CO$_2$ under pressure (400 K, 4–7 atm) followed by acidification gives salicylic acid via electrophilic substitution by CO$_2$.
questions.trick: Kolbe: phenoxide + CO$_2$ (pressure) $\to$ salicylic acid after acidification.

questions.q: Which alcohol, on oxidation with acidified K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$, gives a ketone directly?
questions.explanation: A secondary alcohol has one H on the carbinol carbon and is oxidised to a ketone; primary alcohols give aldehydes/acids, and tertiary alcohols resist oxidation (no α-H).
questions.trick: 2$^\circ$ alcohol (one $\alpha$-H) oxidises to ketone; 1$^\circ$ to acid, 3$^\circ$ resists.

questions.q: Diethyl ether reacts with cold conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ to form
questions.explanation: The lone pair on ether oxygen accepts a proton from H$_2$SO$_4$ to form a protonated oxonium salt, which is why ether dissolves in cold conc. H$_2$SO$_4$.
questions.trick: Ether O lone pair protonates in cold conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ $\to$ oxonium salt.

questions.q: The industrial cumene process for making phenol also yields, as a valuable by-product
questions.explanation: Cumene hydroperoxide, on acid-catalysed rearrangement, cleaves to give phenol and acetone simultaneously.
questions.trick: Cumene process byproduct: phenol + acetone together, always.

questions.q: Reimer–Tiemann reaction on phenol using CHCl$_3$/NaOH followed by acid hydrolysis gives mainly
questions.explanation: Dichlorocarbene generated from CHCl$_3$/NaOH attacks the phenoxide ring ortho to OH; hydrolysis of the resulting dichloromethyl intermediate gives salicylaldehyde.
questions.trick: Reimer-Tiemann: dichlorocarbene attacks phenoxide ortho $\to$ salicylaldehyde.

questions.q: Bromine water reacts with phenol to give
questions.explanation: The OH group strongly activates and directs to o,p positions; with excess Br$_2$ water, all three available positions (2,4,6) are substituted, giving a white precipitate — used as a test for phenol.
questions.trick: Br$_2$ water + phenol $\to$ white ppt of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, classic test.

questions.q: Ethanol and dimethyl ether are functional isomers because
options: they have the same molecular formula but different functional groups
one is aromatic and the other is not
questions.explanation: Both have formula C$_2$H$_6$O, but ethanol has an –OH group while dimethyl ether has a C–O–C linkage; ethanol has a much higher b.p. due to H-bonding.
questions.trick: Same formula, different functional group (OH vs C-O-C) = functional isomers.

questions.q: Dehydration of alcohols to alkenes with hot conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ follows the ease of reaction
questions.explanation: Dehydration proceeds via carbocation formation (E1); tertiary carbocations are most stable and form fastest, so tertiary alcohols dehydrate most readily.
questions.trick: Dehydration via carbocation: ease follows stability, 3$^\circ >$ 2$^\circ >$ 1$^\circ$.

questions.q: Which of the following is the strongest acid?
questions.explanation: The electron-withdrawing –NO$_2$ group stabilises the phenoxide ion by resonance, making p-nitrophenol the strongest acid; electron-donating –CH$_3$ and –OCH$_3$ groups decrease acidity relative to phenol.
questions.trick: Strongest EWG on ring wins acidity: -NO$_2$ beats -OCH$_3$/-CH$_3$ every time.

questions.q: Ethers left standing in contact with air for long periods should not be distilled to dryness because
options: they may form explosive peroxides that concentrate on distillation
they decompose explosively at low temperature
questions.explanation: Ethers slowly autoxidise in air to form unstable peroxides; these are not volatile and become concentrated as the ether distils off, posing an explosion hazard.
questions.trick: Ethers form explosive peroxides in air; never distil an old ether to dryness.

questions.q: Which reagent converts a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol?
questions.explanation: LiAlH$_4$ is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce carboxylic acids (and esters) all the way to primary alcohols; NaBH$_4$ is too weak to reduce acids.
questions.trick: LiAlH$_4$ is strong enough to reduce acids/esters all the way to 1$^\circ$ alcohol.

questions.q: 3 g of an alcohol reacts completely with excess sodium metal to liberate 0.56 L of H$_2$ gas at STP. If the alcohol is monohydric, its molar mass is approximately
questions.explanation: 2ROH + 2Na → 2RONa + H$_2$. Moles of H$_2$ = 0.56/22.4 = 0.025; moles of ROH = 2×0.025 = 0.05. Molar mass = 3/0.05 = 60 g/mol.
questions.trick: 2ROH+2Na$\to$H$_2$: moles H$_2$=V/22.4, moles ROH=2$\times$that, then M=mass/moles.

questions.q: Phenol does not undergo nucleophilic substitution of the OH group easily (unlike alcohols) because
options: phenol is more acidic than alcohols
phenol has no lone pair on oxygen
the C–OH bond in phenol has partial double-bond character due to resonance with the ring
the ring destabilises the leaving hydroxide ion
questions.explanation: Conjugation of the oxygen lone pair with the ring gives the C–O bond partial double-bond character, strengthening it and making OH a poor leaving group in phenol.
questions.trick: Resonance strengthens phenol's C-O bond $\to$ OH is a poor leaving group there.

questions.q: Neutral FeCl$_3$ solution gives a characteristic violet/blue-violet colouration with
questions.explanation: Phenols form coloured complexes with neutral FeCl$_3$ solution (typically violet/blue/green depending on the phenol), a classic qualitative test; alcohols do not give this colour.
questions.trick: Neutral FeCl$_3$ violet colour = phenol test, not alcohols.

questions.q: Which method of alcohol preparation gives an anti-Markovnikov addition of water across a double bond?
options: Hydroboration-oxidation of an alkene (B$_2$H$_6$, then H$_2$O$_2$/NaOH)
Reduction of an aldehyde with NaBH$_4$
questions.explanation: In hydroboration-oxidation, boron adds to the less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov) and is then replaced by OH with retention of configuration, giving the anti-Markovnikov alcohol; acid-catalysed hydration instead follows Markovnikov's rule.
questions.trick: Hydroboration-oxidation gives anti-Markovnikov OH; acid hydration gives Markovnikov OH.

questions.q: Which of these reagents can convert a ketone directly into a tertiary alcohol with two new alkyl groups added?
options: A Grignard reagent, RMgX (2 equivalents needed on an ester, but 1 on a ketone gives a 3° alcohol with one new group)
questions.explanation: A Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon of a ketone; after aqueous work-up this gives a tertiary alcohol bearing the new R group from the Grignard reagent along with the two original substituents from the ketone.
questions.trick: Grignard + ketone $\to$ 3$^\circ$ alcohol; + ester (2 eq.) also gives 3$^\circ$ alcohol.

questions.q: Ortho-nitrophenol is more volatile (has a lower boiling point) than para-nitrophenol mainly because
options: ortho-nitrophenol has intramolecular hydrogen bonding (chelation), reducing intermolecular association, while para-nitrophenol has intermolecular H-bonding, raising its boiling point
para-nitrophenol has a smaller molecular mass
questions.explanation: In o-nitrophenol, the OH and NO$_2$ groups are close enough to form an intramolecular hydrogen bond, which reduces association between molecules and lowers its boiling point and volatility relative to the para isomer, which instead forms intermolecular H-bonds and has a higher boiling point.
questions.trick: Intramolecular H-bond (ortho) lowers b.p.; intermolecular H-bond (para) raises it.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the boiling points of alcohols compared to ethers of similar molar mass?
options: Alcohols have much lower boiling points than ethers because ethers are ionic
Ethers and alcohols of similar molar mass always boil at the same temperature
Ethers always have higher boiling points than alcohols
Alcohols have higher boiling points than ethers of comparable molar mass because alcohols can hydrogen bond with each other, while ethers cannot
questions.explanation: Alcohols possess an O–H group capable of intermolecular hydrogen bonding, which requires more energy to overcome on boiling, whereas ethers (R–O–R') have no O–H and hence weaker dipole-dipole interactions only, giving them lower boiling points.
questions.trick: O-H lets alcohols H-bond each other; ethers can't $\to$ alcohols boil higher.

questions.q: Which of the following alcohols would react FASTEST with Lucas reagent to give an immediate turbidity?
questions.explanation: Lucas reagent (conc. HCl/ZnCl$_2$) reacts via S$_N$1; tertiary alcohols form the most stable carbocation and react (turn turbid) immediately at room temperature.
questions.trick: Most stable carbocation reacts Lucas reagent fastest: tertiary turns turbid instantly.

questions.q: Phenol reacts with zinc dust to give
questions.explanation: When phenol is heated with zinc dust, the C–OH group is removed and replaced by hydrogen (deoxygenation), giving benzene.
questions.trick: Phenol + Zn dust removes C-OH (deoxygenation) $\to$ benzene.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly ranks the acidity of ethanol, water, and phenol from strongest to weakest acid?
questions.explanation: Resonance stabilisation of the phenoxide ion makes phenol the strongest acid of the three; ethanol is the weakest because the ethyl group's +I effect increases electron density on oxygen, disfavouring loss of H$^+$.
questions.trick: Fixed order: phenol $>$ water $>$ ethanol in acid strength.

questions.q: A mixed ether, CH$_3$–O–C(CH$_3$)$_3$ (methyl tert-butyl ether), is heated with excess HI. The major products are expected to be
options: tert-butanol and methyl iodide (S$_N$1 cleavage occurs at the more substituted, tertiary carbon)
tert-butyl alcohol only, with no alkyl iodide
questions.explanation: With a tertiary alkyl group present, ether cleavage by HI proceeds via S$_N$1 at the tertiary carbon (stable carbocation), giving tert-butanol (which may further react) and methyl iodide, rather than cleavage at the less reactive methyl-oxygen bond.
questions.trick: Ether cleavage picks S$_N$1 at the more substituted (tertiary) carbon side.

questions.q: 1.15 g of ethanol (M = 46 g/mol) is completely converted to sodium ethoxide by excess sodium. The volume of H$_2$ gas liberated at STP is
questions.explanation: Moles of ethanol = 1.15/46 = 0.025. From 2ROH + 2Na $\to$ 2RONa + H$_2$, moles of H$_2$ = 0.025/2 = 0.0125. Volume at STP = 0.0125 $\times$ 22.4 = 0.28 L.
questions.trick: 2ROH+2Na$\to$H$_2$: moles H$_2$ = half the moles of alcohol used.

questions.q: Which of the following would NOT give a positive iodoform test?
questions.explanation: n-Propanol lacks a CH$_3$CH(OH)– or CH$_3$CO– group (its OH is on a carbon bearing only one methylene, not a methyl, group with the required substitution pattern), so it does not give the iodoform test, unlike ethanol, isopropanol and acetone.
questions.trick: Iodoform needs CH$_3$CO- or CH$_3$CH(OH)-; n-propanol lacks that methyl-carbinol pattern.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs of compounds are position isomers of the same alcohol formula, C$_4$H$_9$OH?
questions.explanation: 1-Butanol and 2-butanol have the same molecular formula (C$_4$H$_{10}$O) and the same functional group (–OH) but differ in the position of the OH group on the carbon chain, making them position (chain-position) isomers.
questions.trick: Same formula, same group, OH just moved $\to$ position isomers.

questions.q: Which of the following is the correct order of increasing acidity: phenol, o-cresol (o-methylphenol), o-nitrophenol?
questions.explanation: The electron-donating methyl group in o-cresol reduces acidity relative to phenol, while the electron-withdrawing nitro group in o-nitrophenol increases acidity, giving the order o-cresol < phenol < o-nitrophenol.
questions.trick: EDG lowers, EWG raises acidity: cresol $<$ phenol $<$ nitrophenol.

questions.q: The reaction of phenol with dimethyl sulphate in the presence of NaOH gives which class of product?
questions.explanation: Sodium phenoxide is a good nucleophile at oxygen; it reacts with methylating agents like dimethyl sulphate to give the aryl methyl ether (O-alkylation), e.g. phenol to anisole.
questions.trick: Phenoxide O attacks methylating agent (Me$_2$SO$_4$) $\to$ O-alkylation gives aryl ether.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the mechanism of dehydration of a secondary alcohol like 2-butanol with hot conc. H$_2$SO$_4$?
options: E2 with a single concerted step and no intermediate
Protonation of OH, loss of water to form a carbocation, then loss of a $\beta$-hydrogen (E1)
questions.explanation: Acid-catalysed dehydration of 2° and 3° alcohols proceeds via protonation of OH, departure of water to form a carbocation intermediate, and then loss of a proton from a $\beta$-carbon (E1 mechanism) to give the alkene.
questions.trick: 2$^\circ$/3$^\circ$ dehydration: protonate OH, lose water (carbocation), lose $\beta$-H (E1).

questions.q: Which of the following alcohols, upon oxidation with excess acidified KMnO$_4$, gives a carboxylic acid with the SAME number of carbon atoms?
options: A secondary alcohol (gives a ketone, not an acid)
None of these give a carboxylic acid
questions.explanation: A primary alcohol is oxidised first to an aldehyde and then further to a carboxylic acid with strong oxidants like acidified KMnO$_4$, retaining the same carbon skeleton/count.
questions.trick: Only 1$^\circ$ alcohols keep the same carbon count on oxidation to acid.

questions.q: Which statement about the industrial preparation of phenol from chlorobenzene versus from cumene is correct?
options: The Dow process (from chlorobenzene) requires much harsher conditions (623 K, 300 atm) than the more economical cumene process, which is why cumene is now the preferred industrial route
The cumene process requires extremely high pressure and temperature, unlike the Dow (chlorobenzene) process
Neither process is used industrially today
questions.explanation: The chlorobenzene route needs very high temperature and pressure due to the strong, resonance-stabilised C–Cl bond, making it energy-intensive; the cumene process operates under milder conditions and also yields useful acetone as a co-product, making it the economically preferred industrial method.
questions.trick: Cumene process is milder and gives useful acetone; Dow needs harsh 623K/300atm.

questions.q: Which of the following ethers would undergo the FASTEST cleavage with HI, considering steric and electronic factors?
options: Dimethyl ether (least hindered but no special stabilisation)
Di-tert-butyl ether (very hindered, but tertiary carbocation forms via S$_N$1 readily)
Methyl phenyl ether cleaving at the aryl-oxygen bond
questions.explanation: Even though di-tert-butyl ether is sterically hindered for S$_N$2, its tertiary carbon readily forms a stable carbocation, so cleavage proceeds rapidly via S$_N$1; aryl-oxygen bonds (as in anisole) do not cleave at all under these conditions.
questions.trick: Even hindered 3$^\circ$-alkyl ethers cleave fast via S$_N$1 carbocation with HI.

questions.q: Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) is a much stronger acid than phenol because
options: nitro groups donate electron density into the ring
the three electron-withdrawing nitro groups stabilise the phenoxide ion strongly by resonance and induction
questions.explanation: Each nitro group withdraws electron density from the ring by both resonance and induction; with three such groups at positions that can conjugate with the phenoxide oxygen, picric acid's conjugate base is exceptionally stabilised, making it nearly as strong as some mineral acids.
questions.trick: More EWG nitro groups $\to$ stronger phenoxide stabilisation $\to$ picric acid super acidic.

questions.q: Ethanol is denatured (for industrial use, to avoid excise duty on drinking alcohol) typically by adding
options: salt to increase its boiling point
a small amount of sugar to sweeten it
a small amount of a poisonous or nauseating substance such as methanol or pyridine so it becomes unfit for drinking
questions.explanation: Denaturation involves adding substances such as methanol, pyridine, or copper sulphate to ethanol so it becomes unfit for consumption while still usable for industrial and laboratory purposes.
questions.trick: Denaturing = add poisonous/nauseating substance (methanol, pyridine) to spoil drinking use.

questions.q: Which of the following would react with sodium metal to liberate hydrogen gas but would NOT dissolve in aqueous NaOH?
questions.explanation: Both alcohols and phenols react with reactive sodium metal (any O–H bond can do this), but alcohols are far too weakly acidic to be deprotonated by NaOH; phenols (pKa around 10) do dissolve in NaOH, forming soluble sodium phenoxides.
questions.trick: Both react with Na, but only phenols (pKa~10) dissolve in NaOH, not alcohols.

questions.q: When ethanol is heated with excess conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ at 413 K, the major product is
questions.explanation: At the lower temperature of 413 K, with excess ethanol present, intermolecular dehydration dominates: one alcohol molecule's OH is displaced by another's oxygen, giving diethyl ether. Heating further to 443 K instead favours intramolecular dehydration to ethene.
questions.trick: Conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ at 413K $\to$ ether; at 443K (higher T) $\to$ alkene.

questions.q: PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) is a preferred reagent to oxidise a primary alcohol because it gives
options: the aldehyde only, without further oxidation to the acid
questions.explanation: PCC is a mild oxidant used in anhydrous (non-aqueous) conditions, so it stops at the aldehyde stage; strong aqueous oxidants like acidified KMnO$_4$ or K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ would carry the oxidation further to the carboxylic acid.
questions.trick: PCC = mild, anhydrous oxidant: 1$^\circ$ alcohol stops at aldehyde, no further to acid.

questions.q: In glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol), the three –OH groups are classified as
options: one primary and two secondary OH groups
two primary OH groups and one secondary OH group
questions.explanation: Glycerol is HOCH$_2$–CHOH–CH$_2$OH; the terminal carbons (C1, C3) each bear one other carbon so their OH is primary, while the middle carbon (C2), attached to two carbons, carries a secondary OH.
questions.trick: Glycerol: end carbons give 2 primary OH, middle carbon gives 1 secondary OH.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of the ether CH$_3$–CH$_2$–O–CH(CH$_3$)$_2$ is
questions.explanation: The longer chain is propane, with the ethoxy (–OC$_2$H$_5$) group attached at C2 (the isopropyl carbon), giving the IUPAC name 2-ethoxypropane; 'ethyl propyl ether' is only the common (functional class) name.
questions.trick: Name ethers as alkoxy-alkane: locant of O-substituent on the parent chain.

questions.q: When vapours of 2-methylbutan-2-ol (a tertiary alcohol) are passed over heated copper at 573 K, the major product is
questions.explanation: Heated copper dehydrogenates 1° and 2° alcohols (to aldehydes/ketones) because they have an α-hydrogen to remove along with the O–H hydrogen; a tertiary alcohol has no α-H on the carbinol carbon, so it instead undergoes dehydration to give the alkene, 2-methyl-2-butene.
questions.trick: Hot Cu: 1$^\circ\to$aldehyde, 2$^\circ\to$ketone (dehydrogenation); 3$^\circ$ (no $\alpha$-H)$\to$alkene.

questions.q: Given pKa values: ethanol = 15.9, phenol = 10.0, p-nitrophenol = 7.15, picric acid = 0.38, the correct decreasing order of acidity is
questions.explanation: A lower pKa means a stronger acid, so ranking by increasing pKa (0.38, 7.15, 10.0, 15.9) gives decreasing acidity as picric acid > p-nitrophenol > phenol > ethanol, consistent with the number of electron-withdrawing nitro groups stabilising the phenoxide.
questions.trick: Lower pKa = stronger acid; just sort the given pKa values ascending.

questions.q: Treating phenol with excess concentrated HNO$_3$ (with conc. H$_2$SO$_4$) gives mainly
questions.explanation: The strongly activating –OH group directs incoming NO$_2^+$ groups to the o,p positions; with excess concentrated nitrating mixture, all three available o,p positions are nitrated, giving 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid).
questions.trick: Phenol + excess conc. HNO$_3$/H$_2$SO$_4$ $\to$ trinitration at 2,4,6 $\to$ picric acid.

questions.q: Before Kolbe's reaction (treatment with CO$_2$ under pressure) can occur, phenol must first be converted to
questions.explanation: Phenol itself is too weakly nucleophilic at oxygen for the reaction; treating it with NaOH first forms sodium phenoxide, whose more nucleophilic phenoxide ion then attacks CO$_2$ (electrophile) to eventually give salicylic acid after acidification.
questions.trick: Kolbe needs the phenoxide ion (phenol + NaOH first), not phenol itself.

questions.q: Among ethanol, ethylene glycol and glycerol, the highest viscosity is shown by
options: none show any difference in viscosity
questions.explanation: Viscosity increases with the extent of intermolecular hydrogen bonding; glycerol has three –OH groups per molecule, forming the most extensive H-bonded network, making it noticeably more viscous than the diol (glycol) or the monohydric alcohol.
questions.trick: More -OH groups per molecule = more H-bonding = more viscous; glycerol $>$ glycol $>$ ethanol.

questions.q: Allyl alcohol (CH$_2$=CH–CH$_2$OH) reacts with excess HBr to give mainly
questions.explanation: HBr protonates the OH, which leaves as water to generate a resonance-stabilised allylic carbocation; Br$^-$ then attacks this carbocation to substitute the OH, giving allyl bromide, rather than adding across the C=C double bond.
questions.trick: Allylic OH + HX: OH is substituted via the stable allylic carbocation, C=C stays intact.

questions.q: Considering the +I effect of alkyl groups on the basicity (proton-accepting ability) of the oxygen lone pair, the correct order among ether, alcohol and water is
questions.explanation: Each alkyl group attached to oxygen donates electron density inductively, raising the electron density (and hence proton affinity) of the lone pairs on O; an ether has two alkyl groups, an alcohol has one, and water has none, giving the order ether > alcohol > water.
questions.trick: More alkyl groups on O (+I effect) = more electron-rich O = more basic: ether $>$ alcohol $>$ water.

questions.q: Propan-2-ol can be converted to propan-1-ol by which sequence of steps?
options: Oxidation to propanone, then reduction with LiAlH$_4$
Dehydration to propene, then acid-catalysed (Markovnikov) hydration
Direct nucleophilic substitution of OH by H$^-$
questions.explanation: Propan-2-ol is first dehydrated with hot conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ to propene; hydroboration-oxidation (B$_2$H$_6$ then H$_2$O$_2$/NaOH) then adds water anti-Markovnikov, placing OH on the terminal (less substituted) carbon to give propan-1-ol. (Oxidation-reduction via propanone would only regenerate propan-2-ol.)
questions.trick: 2$^\circ\to$1$^\circ$ alcohol: dehydrate to alkene, then hydroborate-oxidise (anti-Markovnikov).

questions.q: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding (chelation) is present in
questions.explanation: In salicylaldehyde, the ortho –OH and the –CHO group are close enough for the OH hydrogen to hydrogen-bond intramolecularly with the carbonyl oxygen, forming a stable six-membered ring; in the para isomer the groups are too far apart, so only intermolecular H-bonding occurs.
questions.trick: Ortho placement of OH next to C=O/COOH $\to$ intramolecular H-bond (chelation).

questions.q: 2.3 g of a monohydric alcohol reacts with excess CH$_3$MgI to liberate 0.56 L of CH$_4$ gas at STP. The molar mass of the alcohol is
questions.explanation: ROH + CH$_3$MgI $\to$ ROMgI + CH$_4$ (1:1). Moles of CH$_4$ = 0.56/22.4 = 0.025 mol = moles of ROH. Molar mass = mass/moles = 2.3/0.025 = 92 g/mol.
questions.trick: ROH + CH$_3$MgI $\to$ CH$_4$ (1:1); moles CH$_4$=V/22.4 gives moles ROH, then M=mass/moles.

questions.q: Diethyl ether is commonly used as the solvent for preparing Grignard reagents because
options: ether reduces the Grignard reagent to an alkane
ether reacts with the Grignard reagent to form an alcohol in situ
the ether oxygen's lone pair coordinates to Mg, solvating and stabilising the Grignard reagent without reacting with it
ether has no interaction at all with the Grignard reagent
questions.explanation: Ether has no acidic O–H to destroy the highly reactive Grignard reagent, but its oxygen lone pair can coordinate to the electron-deficient Mg atom, forming a stabilising solvate complex that keeps the reagent in solution and reactive.
questions.trick: Ether has no O-H to kill RMgX, but its O lone pair solvates the Mg centre.

questions.q: The total number of structurally isomeric alcohols with molecular formula C$_4$H$_{10}$O is
questions.explanation: The four isomeric alcohols are butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol (isobutanol) and 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butanol); dimethyl ether/diethyl ether type structures of this formula are ethers, not alcohols, so are excluded from this count.
questions.trick: C$_4$H$_{10}$O alcohols: 1-butanol, 2-butanol, isobutanol, tert-butanol = 4 isomers.

questions.q: Compared to ethanol, ethylene glycol (ethane-1,2-diol) has a much higher boiling point mainly because
options: ethylene glycol has a much higher boiling point because each molecule can form more intermolecular hydrogen bonds (it has two –OH groups)
ethylene glycol has a lower boiling point due to dipole cancellation
both have nearly identical boiling points since their molar masses are close
ethanol has a higher boiling point because it is a smaller molecule
questions.explanation: Each ethylene glycol molecule carries two –OH groups, so it can participate in a more extensive hydrogen-bonded network than ethanol's single –OH, requiring much more energy to separate the molecules and giving glycol a considerably higher boiling point.
questions.trick: More -OH groups per molecule = more H-bonds = much higher boiling point (glycol $>$ ethanol).

questions.q: The common name of 2,4,6-trinitrophenol is
questions.explanation: 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol is universally known by its common name, picric acid, a strongly acidic yellow solid historically used as an explosive and dye intermediate.
questions.trick: 2,4,6-trinitrophenol's common name is picric acid — remember it directly.

questions.q: In the ceric ammonium nitrate test for the –OH group, alcohols and phenols can be distinguished because
options: alcohols give no colour while phenols turn red
both give an identical yellow colouration
alcohols give a red colouration (complex formation) while phenols give a green colouration
only tertiary alcohols react, all others give no colour
questions.explanation: Ceric ammonium nitrate reacts with the –OH group to form a coloured complex; alcohols characteristically give a red colouration, while phenols give a green colouration, allowing the two classes to be distinguished.
questions.trick: Ceric ammonium nitrate: alcohols turn red, phenols turn green — quick -OH test.

questions.q: The reaction of formaldehyde (HCHO) with a Grignard reagent RMgX, followed by acidic hydrolysis, gives
options: a primary alcohol, since formaldehyde is the least substituted carbonyl compound
questions.explanation: The Grignard reagent's R group adds to the carbonyl carbon of HCHO, which bears no other alkyl substituents, so after aqueous acidic work-up the product is a primary alcohol, R–CH$_2$OH; other aldehydes give secondary alcohols and ketones give tertiary alcohols with a Grignard reagent.
questions.trick: HCHO + RMgX $\to$ 1$^\circ$ alcohol (only formaldehyde does this; other aldehydes give 2$^\circ$).
